topics: Arrangements with identical items or restrictions

items.title: Permutations
items.body: Ordered arrangements: \(^nP_r=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}\). Order matters. \(n\) objects in a line: \(n!\) ways.

items.title: Combinations
items.body: Unordered selections: \(^nC_r=\dbinom{n}{r}=\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\). Order does not matter.

items.title: Restrictions
items.body: Always together: treat as one unit, then \((n-1)!\times r!\). Never together: total − (always together).

items.title: Circular Arrangements
items.body: \((n-1)!\) ways to arrange \(n\) objects in a circle (one position is fixed).

body.en: Permutation (order matters): \(^nP_r=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}\). Combination (order does not matter): \(^nC_r=\dbinom{n}{r}=\dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\). Arrangements with identical items: divide by the factorial of each repeated item. With restrictions: fix the restricted items first, then arrange the rest.

Conditional Probability, Bayes' Theorem & Robust Summary Statistics: For any two events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B) > 0\), conditional probability restricts the sample space to \(B\): \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\). In descriptive statistics, the median and interquartile range (\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\)) are resistant to extreme outliers, whereas the mean \(\bar{x}\) and standard deviation \(s\) are pulled strongly in the direction of skewness.

body.en:
Permutation vs Combination: If order or role matters (e.g. President and Vice President, line order, distinct positions), use permutations \(^nP_r\). If order does not matter (e.g. selecting a committee of 3 students), use combinations \(^nC_r\).

Identical items vs Distinct slots: Arranging \(n\) objects where some are identical requires dividing by each repeat count: \(\frac{n!}{p!\,q!\cdots}\).

'Together' vs 'Separated': For items that must stay together, glue them as a single super-element and arrange \((n - k + 1)!\), then multiply by \(k!\) for internal order. For items that must NEVER be adjacent, arrange the unrestricted items first, creating slots \(\underline{\quad}\star\underline{\quad}\star\dots\), and choose slot positions.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Permutations & Combinations)

body.en:
Why Bayes' Theorem & Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion Work: Any event \(B\) can be partitioned into disjoint intersections \(B = (B \cap A) \cup (B \cap A')\). By additivity of mutually exclusive events and the multiplication rule \(P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)\):

\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid A')P(A')} \]

Similarly, in counting \(|A \cup B|\), summing \(|A| + |B|\) counts every element in \(A \cap B\) twice; subtracting \(|A \cap B|\) once restores exact cardinality: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\).

A committee of 4 is chosen from 5 men and 6 women. Find the number of ways if the committee must contain at least 2 women.

Exactly 2W: \(\binom{6}{2}\binom{5}{2}=15\times10=150\). Exactly 3W: \(\binom{6}{3}\binom{5}{1}=20\times5=100\). Exactly 4W: \(\binom{6}{4}\binom{5}{0}=15\). Total: \(265\).

How many different arrangements are there of the letters of the word BANANA?

6 letters; N appears 2 times, A appears 3 times: \(\dfrac{6!}{3!\,2!}=\dfrac{720}{12}=60\).

label.en: Worked Example C — Permutations & Combinations (Hard Application)

body.en:
Problem (Hard): A geometric progression \( (h_{u}) \) has initial term \( h_1 = 17 \) and common ratio \( r = 2 \). State the fifth term \( h_5 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Using \( h_5 = h_1 r^4 \), we get \( 17 \times 16 = 272 \).

label.en: Worked Example D — Permutations & Combinations (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): An arithmetic progression \( (u_{s}) \) has first term \( u_1 = 18 \) and common difference \( d = 7 \). State the term \( u_{5} \).

Step-by-Step Solution: Using \( u_n = u_1 + (n - 1)d \), we have \( u_{5} = 18 + (5 - 1)(7) = 46 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Permutations & Combinations)

rows.en: Using \(P(A \cap B) = 0\) when told \(A\) and \(B\) are independent
Confuses disjoint (mutually exclusive) events with statistically independent events.
For independent events, multiply probabilities: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)\).
Dividing by the grand total \(N\) when computing \(P(A \mid B)\) from a table
Computes the joint probability \(P(A \cap B)\) instead of conditioning on subset \(B\).
Restrict the denominator strictly to the row/column total of the given condition \(B\).
Using permutations \({}^nP_r\) when selecting a committee with no distinct roles
Overcounts every group of size \(r\) by \(r!\) internal orderings.

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Permutations & Combinations

body.en: Exam Strategy (Cambridge International AS Level (9709 Paper 1 / Paper 4 / Paper 5)): Whenever a probability problem involves "at least one" success across multiple trials, immediately use the Complement Rule: \(P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})\). It turns a multi-case sum into a single calculation.

question.en: In how many ways can 5 people be seated in a row if two particular people (A and B) must not sit next to each other?

solution.en: Total \(=5!=120\). Cases where A & B are adjacent: treat AB as a block → \(4!\times2=48\). Answer: \(120-48=72\).

question.en: Find the number of ways to arrange the 7 letters in the word SUCCESS.

solution.en: The word SUCCESS has 7 letters with 3 S's, 2 C's, 1 U, and 1 E. The number of distinct permutations is \(\frac{7!}{3!\,2!} = \frac{5040}{6 \times 2} = \frac{5040}{12} = 420\).
